learn.title: Hydrogen Fuel Cells in Vehicles
learn.intro: Hydrogen fuel cells are revolutionizing clean transportation by converting hydrogen and oxygen into electricity with only water as exhaust. Unlike batteries, fuel cells can recharge quickly and offer long driving ranges, making them ideal for trucks, buses, and cars aiming to cut emissions without compromising performance.
learn.c1_text: A hydrogen fuel cell works like a continuously replenished battery. Hydrogen flows into the cell and splits into protons and electrons. Electrons travel through a circuit, creating electric current, while protons pass through a membrane. This reaction produces electricity, heat, and pure water—no combustion or pollution.
learn.c2_text: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission aims to make the country a global hub for green hydrogen production and export. With plans to install 5 MMT of hydrogen capacity by 2030, India is investing heavily in hydrogen-powered buses and trucks to decarbonize its transport sector.

learn.stat2: Hydrogen fuel cells are 2x more efficient than internal combustion engines
learn.stat3: FCEVs can refuel in under 5 minutes, matching gasoline cars

learn.title: Flow Batteries for Grid Storage
learn.intro: Flow batteries are transforming how we store renewable energy at grid scale. Unlike traditional lithium-ion batteries, they store energy in liquid electrolytes, allowing for flexible capacity scaling and long-duration discharge—key for balancing solar and wind power when the sun isn't shining or wind isn't blowing.
learn.c1_text: Vanadium flow batteries use vanadium ions dissolved in sulfuric acid as both positive and negative electrolytes. Iron-based systems use iron salts, which are cheaper but less stable. Vanadium offers longer cycle life and better performance, while iron systems promise lower costs for large-scale deployments.
learn.c2_text: India is piloting flow battery projects through SECI to integrate more renewables into the grid. The country's first vanadium flow battery project in Delhi aims to demonstrate 1 MW/4 MWh storage capacity, supporting India's goal of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.

learn.stat2: Vanadium flow batteries last over 20 years with minimal degradation
learn.stat3: Flow batteries can discharge 100% daily without capacity loss
learn.stat4: Global flow battery market expected to reach $942 million by 2027

learn.title: Tidal Stream Energy Basics
learn.intro: Tidal stream energy captures the kinetic power of moving water in oceans and rivers using underwater turbines. Unlike solar and wind, tides are highly predictable decades in advance, making tidal energy a reliable complement to intermittent renewables and a key player in future clean energy grids.
learn.c1_text: Tidal stream turbines work like underwater wind turbines, harnessing the force of tidal currents. These axial or cross-flow turbines convert kinetic energy from moving water into electricity. With water being 800x denser than air, even slow currents generate significant power efficiently.
learn.c2_text: India has identified 300 GW of ocean energy potential along its 7,500 km coastline. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy is supporting pilot projects in Tamil Nadu and Kerala to test tidal and wave energy technologies, aiming to commercialize ocean energy by 2030.

learn.stat2: Water is 800 times denser than air, boosting turbine efficiency

learn.title: Green Bonds for Renewable Projects
learn.intro: Green bonds are specialized financial instruments that fund climate-positive projects like solar farms, wind parks, and grid modernization. As renewable energy transitions accelerate, green bonds have become a crucial tool for mobilizing private capital toward a low-carbon future and meeting global climate goals.
learn.c1_text: Green bonds raise capital specifically for environmental projects. Investors receive returns while funding solar installations, wind farms, or battery storage. In 2023, over $500 billion in green bonds were issued globally, helping bridge the $4 trillion annual clean energy investment gap needed to reach net-zero by 2050.
learn.c2_text: India issued its first sovereign green bond in 2023, raising $1 billion for renewable energy and sustainable infrastructure. The country plans to issue $10 billion in green bonds by 2025, supporting its target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity and aligning with its $10 trillion climate commitment by 2070.

learn.title: Solar Inverter Types Explained
learn.intro: Solar inverters convert the DC electricity produced by solar panels into AC electricity used in homes and businesses. Choosing the right inverter type—string, micro, or hybrid—affects system efficiency, cost, and energy independence. Understanding these options is essential for optimizing rooftop solar performance.
learn.c1_text: String inverters connect multiple panels in series, offering low cost but reduced performance if one panel is shaded. Microinverters attach to each panel individually, maximizing output even with partial shading. For a typical 6 kW rooftop system, microinverters can boost energy yield by 5–25% compared to string setups.
learn.c2_text: India's solar pump and rooftop programs emphasize hybrid inverters for rural electrification. Over 1.5 million solar pumps use string inverters, while urban rooftop projects increasingly adopt microinverters. The government's PM-KUSUM scheme supports inverter upgrades to improve agricultural sector energy efficiency.
learn.stat1: India has installed over 80 GW of solar capacity as of 2024

learn.title: Solar PV and the Photoelectric Effect
learn.intro: Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using the photoelectric effect—a phenomenon where photons knock electrons loose from semiconductor materials. This clean, silent technology powers everything from rooftop homes to utility-scale solar farms, making it the world's fastest-growing energy source.
learn.c1_text: When sunlight hits a solar cell, photons with enough energy dislodge electrons from silicon atoms. This creates electron-hole pairs that generate direct current (DC). Metal conductive plates on the cell collect this current and transfer it through wires, producing usable electricity without moving parts or noise.
